nodes.text: A barrier to communication is anything that interferes with the ability of employees to convey information in a timely and accurate manner; strategies to overcome communication barriers are direct or indirect.[^1] Cultural barriers arise from different cultural backgrounds, including generational barriers, and can lead to cultural clashes.[^2] Linguistic barriers include different languages and jargon.[^3] Emotional barriers such as anger or frustration, and psychological and physiological barriers such as fear of public speaking, make it harder to convey information.[^4] Physical barriers include closed doors, being unable to reach senior managers, noisy open-plan offices and faulty equipment.[^5] Organisational barriers arise when many levels of hierarchy or a long chain of command delay information transfer.[^6] Other barriers are attitude and personality, perception, technological barriers, the communication skills of sender and receiver, and an inappropriate form of communication.[^7] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.6 lists it under: define (AO1); explain (AO2).[^8]

nodes.text: Collective bargaining is when employees work together with management to negotiate wages and working conditions.[^1] It can occur through formal trade unions, and also where no formal union is present.[^2] For workers it gives more power together than as individuals, and for the business it means negotiating with one group, with all workers abiding by the agreement.[^3] Its failure can lead to more significant industrial action by employees or employers.[^4] Where union membership is lower, collective bargaining is usually more difficult to implement.[^5] P&O Ferries chose not to consult unions because it saw no chance that collective bargaining would result in a solution.[^6] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.7 lists it under: define (AO1).[^7]

nodes.text: A cultural clash occurs when more than one culture within a business competes for dominance and conflict results.[^1] Cultural clashes are likely to be a hygiene factor causing dissatisfaction, low motivation and higher labour turnover.[^2] They can cause confusion over expectations, lower productivity and higher costs.[^3] Cultural disharmony can impede creativity, and raising cultural awareness of biases and assumptions can reduce it.[^4] Circumstances include growth, a change in leadership and multinational expansion.[^5] External growth almost always involves cultural tensions, and culture clash is a leading reason why it can fail, as in Amazon's acquisition of Whole Foods.[^6] A new leader with a different style can clash with a team used to democratic leadership, as the loss of autonomy and voice is demotivating.[^7] Multinational expansion carries a particular risk of culture clash through differences in national culture such as language, working habits, relationships and ethical norms.[^8] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.5 lists it under: define (AO1); discuss (AO3).[^9]

nodes.text: Edward Deci and Richard Ryan published Intrinsic Motivation and Self-determination in Human Behaviour in 1985.[^1] They described three factors that drive intrinsic motivation: autonomy, competence and relatedness.[^2] Autonomy refers to the ability of a person to make decisions and to be independent.[^3] Competence refers to a feeling of capability to do things in the world, and relatedness to a feeling of connection with other people.[^4] Extrinsic motivators such as bonuses can undermine intrinsic motivation.[^5] Its implications for competence are basically the same as for achievement-oriented employees in McClelland's acquired needs theory.[^6] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.4 lists it under: discuss (AO3).[^7]

nodes.text: Employee-employer relations are the manner in which employees and employers treat each other.[^1] Employers have a moral duty to provide decent working conditions, fair pay and a safe working environment, and employees have a duty to be loyal and respectful.[^2] A breakdown can lead to a poor reputation, demotivated employees, high labour turnover, inability to recruit and disruption to operations.[^3] Good relations can be a source of competitive advantage by helping retain skilled employees and attract recruits.[^4] The International Labour Organisation lists wages, conditions of work, work-life balance, non-discrimination, protection from harassment and purposeful work as crucial elements.[^5] Stakeholders are interdependent, yet there are often conflicts between them.[^6] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.7 lists it under: explain (AO2).[^7]

nodes.text: John Stacey Adams published his equity theory in 1963, claiming that satisfaction and motivation in the workplace are determined by understanding of fairness.[^1] Fairness relates to the ratio of inputs, such as time, effort and expertise, to outcomes, such as compensation, recognition and sense of achievement.[^2] An imbalance, or perceived unfairness compared with colleagues, may lead to dissatisfaction and demotivation.[^3] It implies that businesses should address inequity such as gender pay discrepancies and examine executive pay more carefully.[^4] It and expectancy theory are both focused on processes rather than needs.[^5] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.4 lists it under: discuss (AO3).[^6]

nodes.text: Frederick Herzberg published The Motivation to Work in 1959, formulating the two-factor theory from interviews with about 200 accountants and engineers.[^1] It proposes hygiene factors that cause job dissatisfaction and motivators that cause job satisfaction, so removing dissatisfaction does not by itself create satisfaction.[^2] Higher order needs, such as psychological and self-fulfilment needs, are treated as motivators.[^3] Compensation is a hygiene factor, so inadequate pay can cause dissatisfaction even where motivators are present.[^4] The theory is similar to Maslow's hierarchy of needs in identifying basic needs, and seems to work well with a democratic leadership style.[^5] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.4 lists it under: discuss (AO3).[^6]

nodes.text: Hofstede described a study of IBM employees in more than 60 countries in his 2001 book Culture's Consequences.[^1] The dimensions for analysing national culture are power distance, uncertainty avoidance, individualism versus collectivism, masculinity versus femininity, long-term versus short-term orientation and indulgence versus restraint.[^2] Power distance is the extent to which people accept a hierarchical power structure; low power distance means more bottom-up communication and less hierarchy.[^3] Uncertainty avoidance is the tolerance for risk and ambiguity; risk-averse countries tend to have tighter rules and formal chains of command.[^4] Individualistic societies such as the USA are more likely to use performance-related pay, while collectivist societies value the common good.[^5] Masculine values include financial rewards and competition, while feminine values include wellbeing and sharing, which may affect flexible working conditions.[^6] Long-term orientation is associated with patient strategies, and short-term orientation with pressure for revenue and cost cutting.[^7] Indulgence versus restraint is the extent to which a society lets people freely satisfy basic drives for fun and enjoying life.[^8] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.5 lists it under: apply (AO2).[^9]

nodes.text: Industrial action is a form of protest that puts pressure on the other party to resolve a dispute.[^1] Employee actions include work-to-rule, overtime ban and strike action.[^2] Employer tactics include collective bargaining, redundancy, contract changes, closures and lock-outs.[^3] Industrial action tends to escalate complicated situations and can be damaging for both sides, though at times it is the only way to break an impasse.[^4] Shared downsides are increased costs, lost output and revenue, reputation damage, damaged relationships and possible job losses.[^5] Employees may find it hard to take part if they are not unified, or if the action is not protected by law.[^6] The political, social and legal situation of a country affects which methods of industrial action are used.[^7]

nodes.text: The Laloux Culture Model comes from Frederic Laloux's 2014 book Reinventing Organizations.[^1] It suggests five types of organisational culture associated with levels and colours, each linked to a leadership style or management philosophy.[^2] Red organisations concentrate power in one or a few people who keep it through fear, as in gangs or the mafia.[^3] Amber organisations are like the military, with strict hierarchy and chains of command, and suit stable and predictable environments.[^4] Orange organisations are like machines, results-oriented, competitive and growth-oriented, such as many large corporations.[^5] Green organisations are like families, motivated by shared purpose and value for a wide range of stakeholders, though they still have a hierarchy.[^6] Teal organisations are like living organisms, with decentralised power, self-managed employees and trust to make significant decisions.[^7] Laloux treats Teal organisations as highly evolved, but different organisations need different cultures, and the military would find Teal difficult.[^8] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.5 lists it under: analyse (AO2).[^9]

nodes.text: Abraham Maslow developed his hierarchy of needs in 1943, claiming that some needs have to be satisfied before others can be met.[^1] From the bottom, the levels are physiological needs, safety and security needs, love and belonging needs, esteem needs and self-actualisation needs.[^2] Maslow believed people must satisfy basic needs before psychological needs, and psychological needs before self-fulfilment needs.[^3] If the theory is correct, businesses can meet employees' basic needs so that they can meet psychological and self-fulfilment needs, becoming happier, more motivated and more productive.[^4] The pyramid shape was added later by other theorists; Maslow did not use a pyramid when he published his theory.[^5] The syllabus checklist for subtopic 2.4 lists it under: discuss (AO3).[^6]
